headline: Viruses challenge our definition of life—they can't reproduce alone but can evolve and spread
universal_truth: Boundaries are often blurry; clear categories sometimes fail to capture reality
fun_facts: Viruses are 100 times smaller than bacteria—too small to see with ordinary microscopes
About 8% of human DNA came from ancient viral infections—viruses are part of our genome
There are an estimated 10 million trillion trillion viruses on Earth—more than any other entity
discussion_questions: How can something that can't reproduce alone evolve?
What does the virus debate teach us about defining life?

hook.script: Are viruses alive? They have genetic material, they evolve, they spread. But they can't reproduce alone—they need to hijack living cells. Viruses occupy a strange space: not quite dead, not quite alive. They challenge our categories.

cliff.script: Living things reproduce, metabolize, and respond to their environment. Viruses don't metabolize or reproduce independently—they're inert crystals until they contact a cell. So why do we treat them like life?
cliff.prompt: Why are viruses so hard to classify?

options.text: They have some properties of life (genetic code, evolution) but lack others (metabolism, independent reproduction)
options.response: Yes. Viruses are at the edge of our definition. They blur the line between chemistry and biology, forcing us to ask what 'alive' really means.

options.text: Scientists haven't agreed on a definition of life yet
options.response: True, but viruses specifically highlight the boundary problem...

fact1.title: Hijackers
fact1.script: Viruses can't reproduce alone. They inject their genetic material into cells, which then follow viral instructions—producing more viruses. The cell does the work. The virus provides only information—a genetic blueprint that hijacks cellular machinery.

fact2.title: Ancient Invaders
fact2.script: About 8% of your DNA came from viruses—ancient infections that got incorporated into our ancestors' genomes. Some of this viral DNA is essential for human biology. Viruses have been editing life for billions of years.

fact3.title: Overwhelming Numbers
fact3.script: There are more viruses on Earth than any other biological entity—an estimated 10 million trillion trillion. They infect every form of life, from bacteria to whales. Despite not quite being alive, viruses are everywhere.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Boundaries are often blurry. Viruses teach that clear categories sometimes fail to capture reality. 'Alive or not' may be the wrong question—reality resists our either/or thinking.

outro.script: That's Day 150—150 days of learning together! That's nearly half a year! Tomorrow, we'll explore how nature connects. Until then, consider how viruses challenge our simplest categories.

growTrack.title: Boundary Questioning - Embrace Ambiguity
growTrack.activity: Find something in your life that doesn't fit neatly into categories—a relationship, a belief, a situation. Viruses remind us that 'either/or' thinking has limits. Some things just are what they are, regardless of our labels.
